title: How Close Can a Supernova Get Before It Destroys Earth?

sentences.text: Could a dying star explode near our solar system and rip Earth's atmosphere away into space?
Science fiction movies often show a fiery blast wave sweeping our planet entirely bare within seconds.
This question matters to you because that fragile layer of air makes all terrestrial life possible.
Without an atmosphere to provide oxygen, survival would be impossible.
In reality, a supernova is an unimaginably powerful explosion marking the death of a star.
When a massive star runs out of fuel, its core collapses under immense gravitational force.
Alternatively, an exploding white dwarf star undergoes runaway nuclear fusion.
These stellar detonations expel several solar masses of matter into the surrounding interstellar medium.
The ejected material travels outward at speeds reaching several per cent of the speed of light.
This creates an expanding shock wave that sweeps up a shell of interstellar gas and dust.
Yet space is so vast that this physical debris spreads out across dozens of light-years.
By the time it reaches us, the physical blast wave cannot blow away our planetary air.
Where are the nearest stars that might explode in our stellar neighbourhood?
Astronomers define a near-Earth supernova as one occurring within roughly 33 to 978 light-years.
At present, our galaxy contains up to 14 near-Earth supernova candidates within that wider distance.
Several prominent stars within a few hundred light-years could explode in as little as 1,000 years.
Although these dying stars will shine brilliantly, they pose little direct threat to our planet.
Take the famous red supergiant Betelgeuse, which fascinates skywatchers.
Scientists estimate that Betelgeuse may take up to 1.5 million years to undergo a supernova.
When it finally detonates, its stream of charged particles will take 100,000 years to reach Earth.
Looking back in time, other relatively nearby stars have exploded without harming our biosphere.
The Vela supernova exploded about 12,000 years ago roughly 800 light-years away from our Sun.
Another explosion called Geminga occurred roughly 300,000 years ago at a distance of 550 light-years.
The closest known white dwarf candidate, IK Pegasi, is currently moving away to a safe distance.
If a blast wave cannot destroy our atmosphere, what makes a supernova dangerous?
The real threat comes from invisible electromagnetic radiation travelling across interstellar space at light speed.
Supernovae act as primary cosmic factories, generating immense amounts of high-energy cosmic rays.
They also emit intense pulses of penetrating X-rays and highly energetic gamma rays.
Gamma rays are responsible for most of the catastrophic damage to any life-bearing terrestrial world.
When gamma radiation strikes the upper atmosphere, it does not push the gases into space.
Instead, these energetic photons cause radiolysis of diatomic nitrogen and diatomic oxygen molecules.
Radiolysis breaks apart these common gas molecules and recombines them into harmful nitrogen oxides.
These newly created nitrogen oxides act as powerful catalysts that rapidly destroy ozone molecules.
In this way, the star uses invisible chemistry to dismantle our planet's vital stratospheric shield.
The air remains bound to Earth, but its protective composition is transformed.
Invisible atomic reactions take the place of the Hollywood shockwave.
How close must a star be for this lethal chemistry to occur?
Scientists calculate that the genuine danger zone begins within a few dozen light-years of Earth.
An explosion within 33 light-years happens on average only once every 240 million years.
If a Type 2 supernova explodes closer than 26 light-years, severe damage follows.
At this lethal distance, the incoming radiation would destroy more than half of Earth's ozone layer.
Researchers derived this calculation from atmospheric models and radiation data from supernova 1987A.
Type 1a supernovae can be even more dangerous to our planet if they occur nearby.
These events occur when an exploding white dwarf releases tremendous energy within mere seconds.
At peak brightness, such an explosion can shine 5 billion times brighter than our Sun.
Because white dwarfs are dim and common, they can detonate unpredictably in unstudied systems.
Any stellar detonation occurring inside 30 light-years would cross the critical threshold of survival.
That narrow boundary represents the cosmic line where atmospheric protection completely collapses.
What happens to the world below when half of the ozone layer is wiped out?
Ozone is the only atmospheric gas capable of absorbing dangerous ultraviolet B radiation from sunlight.
When stratospheric ozone levels drop, intense ultraviolet B light penetrates directly to the surface.
This extreme radiation damages cellular DNA, causing pyrimidine bases to form transcription errors during replication.
In humans and animals, excess ultraviolet exposure causes severe skin cancers and cataracts.
Marine ecosystems suffer catastrophic harm because ultraviolet rays penetrate into shallow waters.
Phytoplankton and delicate coral reef communities are particularly vulnerable to this sudden radiation spike.
Their collapse would severely deplete the base of the marine food chain.
At the same time, elevated cosmic rays can alter climate patterns and cool the global temperature.
Gamma ray bursts from dangerously close stars may have caused the ancient end-Ordovician extinction.
That prehistoric cataclysm resulted in the death of nearly 60 per cent of all oceanic life.
Rapid successive supernovae have also been proposed as triggers for the Late Devonian extinction.

scenes.heading: Ocean Floor Clues and the Final Verdict

sentences.text: Did nearby exploding stars actually bombard our planet during geological history?
The definitive proof came not from looking upward, but by digging deep into the seabed.
Dying stars forge heavy elements and disperse them into space during their catastrophic final moments.
One isotope created in these events is iron-60, with a half-life of 2.62 million years.
Researchers examining deep-sea rocks in the Pacific Ocean discovered 23 atoms of this rare isotope.
They identified these stellar atoms within the top two centimetres of the oceanic crust.
This detection proves an explosion occurred within the last 5 million years.
The recovered iron indicates the dying star exploded less than 98 light-years away.
Similar interstellar traces have also appeared in Antarctic surface snow and in lunar samples.
Iron-60 atoms were even found preserved inside fossilised bacteria living in seabed sediments.
So how close would a dying star need to be to wipe out our protective atmospheric shield?
A supernova does not blow away our air, but one inside 26 to 33 light-years destroys our ozone layer.
Lethal gamma rays convert atmospheric oxygen into nitrogen oxides, stripping away our shield through invisible chemistry.
Next time you gaze at the night sky, consider the fragile invisible balance protecting our world.
